title: Strong $O$-valued contextuality: ruling out discrete nondeterministic alternatives to quantum theory
abstract: Gleason's theorem identifies the Born rule via non-contextuality over an infinite continuous lattice of projectors, while its corollary the Kochen-Specker (KS) theorem rules out the specific class of deterministic ($\{0,1\}$-valued) noncontextual models using finite sets of projectors. Gleason's theorem also indicates the existence of KS-type finite vector constructions to rule out other discrete nondeterministic alternatives to quantum theory beyond the $\{0, 1\}$ case. Here, we construct finite measurement configurations to rule out noncontextual empirical models with outcome probabilities drawn from an arbitrary finite subset $O \subset [0,1]$. We do this by two means: (i) constructing a family of experimentally feasible state-dependent Hardy-type tests, and (ii) proving a generalized KS theorem for a broad class of $O$ that includes prior results as special cases. In the sheaf-theoretic framework of Abramsky and Brandenburger, a hierarchy of probabilistic-possibilistic-strong contextuality has been established quantifying contextuality as a resource. We extend this framework by introducing strong $O$-valued contextuality, showing that quantum theory evades global sections of all finite-valued presheaves. We also discuss the implications of the result on finite many-valued logics as viable ontological models for quantum theory and for contextuality-based (semi)-device-independent protocols.
summary: The paper generalizes the Kochen-Specker theorem by constructing finite tests to rule out noncontextual models where outcome probabilities are drawn from any arbitrary finite set O. Using sheaf theory and logical gadgets, it proves that quantum mechanics exhibits 'strong $O$-valued contextuality,' demonstrating that such discrete alternatives cannot consistently describe quantum measurements.
main_problem: To construct finite measurement configurations that rule out noncontextual empirical models whose outcome probabilities are drawn from an arbitrary finite subset O of [0,1], thereby generalizing the Kochen-Specker theorem.
main_result: The paper proves a generalized KS theorem showing that quantum theory evades global sections of all finite-valued presheaves defined over such $O$-valued assignments. This rules out many-valued logics as viable ontological models for quantum mechanics.
method: The authors employ sheaf theory, propositional logic (Compactness Theorem), and construct specific 'gadgets' involving vector sets in $\mathbb{C}^3$ to derive contradictions from assumed context-independent probability assignments.
model_or_system: The focus is on quantum measurements represented by projectors $P \in \mathcal{P}(H)$ on a Hilbert space, testing noncontextual models where outcome probabilities are restricted to an arbitrary finite set $O$.
key_observables: Contextuality itself, quantified by the failure of global assignments $\lambda_O: V 	o O$ to satisfy structural constraints derived from measurement compatibility.
important_parameters: The structure of the allowed value set $O$, particularly when it includes 0 and 1, and the dimension of the Hilbert space ($d \ge 3$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that any alternative theory must assign probabilities from a finite set $O$ to all measurements, allowing for the application of logical compactness arguments.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate specific 'gadget' graphs (e.g., nested Clifton graph) used in the proof structure to enforce constraints on assignments, leading to contradictions when assuming context-independent values.
paper_structure: The paper builds from Gleason's theorem and KS theorem by first introducing $O$-valued valuations. It then develops constructive tests using Hardy-type measurements (Chunk 2), culminating in a formal proof using sheaf theory and propositional logic gadgets (Chunks 3 & 4) to establish the generalized KS theorem for finite $O$.
why_interesting: This work provides deep mathematical constraints on the structure of quantum reality, showing that even if one restricts possible outcomes to discrete values beyond $\{0,1\}$, contextuality remains a necessary feature.
